title: Rattan Singh Bhangu
hookLine: his Panth Prakash told the Khalsa's hard century in verse

lines: THE SIKH SIDE, TOLD BY A SIKH.
cards: A Sikh sits down to write. Not in prose. In verse, line after line that can be read aloud and remembered.
He has the stories his family told him: the riders and the forests, the great killing, the temple blown up and rebuilt. Some of them are about his own family.
And, by his own account, he has a reason to write: outsiders are asking about the Sikhs, and he wants the Sikh side told by a Sikh.

teach.h: PANTH PRAKASH: THE PATH BROUGHT TO LIGHT.
teach.b: First, the book. It's called Panth Prakash. Panth is the path, and the word Sikhs use for the whole community.
Prakash is light, the shining of something into view. So the title promises to bring the Panth into the light. Second, why he wrote it.

teach.h: WRITTEN SO THE SIKH SIDE WAS TOLD.
teach.b: Bhangu says a British officer was collecting accounts of Sikh history, and that he heard the Sikhs described by people who didn't know them. So he set out to tell it from inside. That's a choice worth noticing.
He didn't write an angry reply.

teach.h: HIS OWN FAMILY IN THE STORY.
teach.b: He wrote the long story, with names, places and family memory, so it would be there for anyone who asked. Third, his family is in it.
Bhangu traces his line to Mehtab Singh, one of the riders remembered for punishing the man who had turned the Harmandir into a place of drinking and dancing.
So when he tells the hard century, he's telling his own family's world. Fourth, how to read him.
Because he wrote later, from memory and family tradition, historians read him carefully, beside other sources: yesterday's lesson in action.
And yet several stories on this path in recent weeks, Kapur Singh fanning the sangat, the boy Jassa Singh singing, the shaheedi bunga, are told in the forms Sikhs know through tellings like his.
When this path says tradition says, Bhangu is one of the voices in that tradition.

how: Rattan Singh Bhangu's Panth Prakash is read by Sikh historians and drawn on in gurdwara katha about the eighteenth century, alongside other sources.

practice: Find or recall one line of history, a sentence from a book, a plaque on a building, an inscription on a gravestone, the first line of a page about where your family came from, and read it slowly, once.
Then put it down, breathe, and ask who wrote it, and where they were standing. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.
